name: Vbeam Perfecta

lead: Vbeam Perfecta is a pulsed dye laser from Candela used by dermatologists for port-wine stains, hemangiomas, broken capillaries and persistent facial redness. People seek it for a calmer, more even complexion, and some practices offer it for scars.

The 595 nm light is absorbed by hemoglobin, heating and closing small vessels, while a cryogen spray cools the skin surface during each pulse. Pulsed dye lasers have long been treated in the medical literature as the standard approach for port-wine stains. Studies of it for general appearance, such as photoaging, are small.

paras: It is done in a clinic, usually as a series of sessions weeks apart. Settings can be chosen to reduce bruising, and treated redness fades over the following days to weeks. Results build across sessions.

Bruising (purpura) and temporary redness or swelling are recognized effects; settings such as pulse stacking have been studied to reduce purpura. People often plan around visible marks for a period after treatment.

angle.text: Vbeam's 595-nm light is absorbed by blood, closing visible vessels and reducing facial redness for a calmer complexion. It is used for broken capillaries, rosacea-related flushing and some scars, and is well established for vascular lesions.

lead: Vbeam Perfecta is a pulsed dye laser (PDL) system made by Candela that emits yellow light at 595 nm, a wavelength absorbed by hemoglobin. It is used in dermatology for vascular lesions such as port-wine stains, hemangiomas, facial telangiectasias and rosacea-related redness, and some practices offer it for scars and general facial redness [1].

Pulsed dye lasers have long been treated in the medical literature as the standard approach for port-wine stains [2][3]. Evidence for purely cosmetic uses, such as photoaging, is limited to small studies [4].
infobox: Variable pulse duration; cryogen Dynamic Cooling Device [1]

paras: According to an AI-generated encyclopedia entry, Candela introduced its first pulsed dye laser in the 1980s, developed from selective photothermolysis work done with Massachusetts General Hospital, and the Vbeam line followed in the early 2000s, with the Perfecta model launched in 2005 [1].
The same source describes a 595 nm wavelength, adjustable pulse durations of roughly 0.45 to 40 ms, spot sizes of about 3 to 12 mm and a cryogen spray cooling device that protects the epidermis [1].

In selective photothermolysis the laser light is absorbed by oxyhemoglobin, heating and closing targeted vessels while sparing surrounding tissue [1]. Variable pulse settings, including stacking multiple lower-fluence pulses, have been studied as a way to heat vessels while reducing purpura (bruising) [5].

The practical appeal of a pulsed dye laser is that it targets blood vessels, so it is used where visible redness is the problem: port-wine stains, facial telangiectasias (small surface vessels), diffuse redness from rosacea, and red or pink scars.[1][6][7] People seeking a more even complexion book it for the appearance of persistent facial redness; the visible result they aim for is a lighter, more uniform skin tone once the treated vessels close down.[1]

A multicenter phase 4 study of 46 people with moderate to severe rosacea redness used one of four energy-based devices, including the Vbeam Perfecta, plus an oxymetazoline cream between sessions, and tracked clinician erythema scores, tolerability and satisfaction in an open-label design.[6] A registered 34-person trial examined pulsed dye laser together with oxymetazoline for erythematotelangiectatic rosacea.[8]

Dye lasers were first demonstrated in 1966, and pulsed, tunable versions made it possible to match emission to the absorption peaks of hemoglobin or melanin, which is why the technology moved into dermatology for port-wine stains and other vascular lesions, scars and tattoo removal.[9] The Vbeam family is a commercial 595 nm flashlamp-pumped variant of this idea.[1]

Most published work concerns medical vascular indications rather than appearance enhancement in healthy skin. A randomized comparison of treatment with the pulsed dye laser versus wait-and-see for superficial infantile hemangioma has been published [2]. Port-wine stains are described in the literature as a condition where PDL is considered the gold standard, although a large share of lesions may be refractory, prompting trials of add-ons such as topical rapamycin [3].

A randomized trial of a 595-nm laser examined fresh surgical scars [7], and a blinded randomized trial using a 595-nm laser to create bruises tested whether topical arnica hastened bruise resolution [10]. A pulse-stacking study examined whether stacked low-fluence pulses affect outcomes in vascular lesions [5].
Registered trials include a 20-person study of the Vbeam Prima for photoaged facial skin [4] and a 34-person study combining PDL with oxymetazoline cream for erythematotelangiectatic rosacea [8].

A prospective study of 22 people with untreated port-wine stains compared the Vbeam with Candela's Cynergy, another 595 nm pulsed dye platform, treating the same patients with both to compare efficacy and safety.[11] A report of two children with port-wine stains and darker skin types described successful treatment with a 595 nm laser, addressing a population often underrepresented in laser studies.[12]

A side-by-side study examined whether EMLA numbing cream changed either the efficacy of PDL for port-wine stains or the pain experienced, finding the cream did not alter efficacy or pain reduction.[13]

Bruising (purpura) is a recognized effect of pulsed dye laser treatment, and several studies and cooling features aim to reduce it [5][10]. Descriptions of the device note that cryogen cooling is intended to lessen discomfort and protect the epidermis [1].

Purpura, bruising after a pulse, is the most characteristic temporary effect and is the reason low-fluence stacked pulses and long pulse durations are studied.[5][10] A trial of 20 percent topical arnica after laser-induced bruising evaluated whether it speeds bruise resolution.[10]

timeline.event: Candela's early pulsed dye laser reportedly receives FDA clearance for vascular lesions (per Grokipedia). [1]
